extracted.intended_audience: Washington Post journalists, editors, contributors and newsroom staff
extracted.subtask_description: Organizational policies and standards governing Washington Post journalism: editorial ethics, sourcing, verification, corrections, conflicts of interest, treatment of sources, opinion labeling, social media conduct, diversity and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth as nearly as the truth may be ascertained
rubrics_metrics.description: The first mission of a newspaper is to tell the truth as nearly as the truth may be ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational principle guiding reporting and editing; reporters and editors should pursue accuracy and transparency in establishing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell ALL the truth about important affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper shall tell ALL the truth so far as it can learn it, concerning the important affairs of America and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting should aim for completeness on matters of public significance; omission of major facts undermines fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe decencies obligatory upon a private gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: As a disseminator of the news, the paper shall observe the decencies that are obligatory upon a private gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism should respect standards of civility and decorum appropriate to public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content fit for readers young and old
rubrics_metrics.description: What it prints shall be fit reading for the young as well as for the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience sensibilities across age groups when deciding content and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to readers and the public, not owners' private interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper’s duty is to its readers and to the public at large, and not to the private interests of its owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should prioritize public interest and independence from ownership influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to sacrifice material fortunes for the public good
rubrics_metrics.description: In the pursuit of truth, the newspaper shall be prepared to make sacrifices of its material fortunes, if such course be necessary for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial independence may require costly choices; financial considerations must not override public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not be an ally of special interests; be fair and wholesome
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper shall not be the ally of any special interest, but shall be fair and free and wholesome in its outlook on public affairs and public men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid alignment with special interests; maintain fairness and balanced perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: This news organization is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflict of interest wherever and whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key rules include: pay our own way; accept no gifts from news sources (occasional innocent invitations are exceptions); accept no free trips; do not accept payment/honoraria/expenses from governments or entities we cover; avoid accepting money from individuals or organizations that lobby or try to influence issues we cover; be wary of entanglement with likely subjects of coverage; avoid active partisan involvement; disclose household/family business or professional ties to department heads. Exceptions are few and must be handled cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors of The Post are committed to fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness entails completeness (not omitting facts of major importance), relevance (not including irrelevant info at expense of significant facts), honesty (not misleading readers), and offering covered individuals/organizations the opportunity to address assertions — diligently seek comment and consider it genuinely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post respects taste and decency and shall avoid prurience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid profanities and obscenities unless their use is essential to a significant story (approval required by executive/managing editors). Use visual/text warnings for potentially offensive material. Do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity; consult Legal if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and labeling of Opinion/Analysis/Perspective/Review
rubrics_metrics.description: The separation of news columns from the editorial pages is solemn and complete; analysis, perspective, opinion and review must be plainly labeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Analysis = interpretation based on evidence; Perspective = discussion with a point of view or first-person narratives; Opinion = column or blog in Opinions section; Review = critic’s assessment. Labels help readers distinguish facts from interpretation/opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: When using networks such as Facebook, Twitter etc., for reporting or for our personal lives, we must protect our professional integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts reflect on the newsroom; treat every comment/link as public; refrain from posting anything that could objectively be perceived as reflecting political, racial, sexist, religious or other bias or favoritism; maintain reputation for excellence, fairness and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: National and community interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is vitally concerned with the national interest and with the community interest and believes these are best served by wide dissemination of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims by officials that something is in the national/community interest do not automatically equate; exercise independent judgment about public interest when deciding coverage and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: A journalist's role: report, don't make the news; do not misrepresent identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should make every effort to remain in the audience, to be the stagehand rather than the star, to report the news, not to make the news; do not misrepresent identity or occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not portray oneself as police, physicians, etc.; reporting should be honorable and defensible publicly; do not mislead sources about who you are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact-checking standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing, and fact-checking their stories; stories are subject to review by one or more editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-level review can involve assignment editors, multiplatform/copy editors, and senior editors; the number and extent of editor review varies by complexity, sensitivity and time pressure. Editors for digital platforms may also influence presentation, headlines, alerts and newsletters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is at the core of Washington Post journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate reporting requires engaging a variety of voices as interviewees and writers, striving for staff that reflects diverse backgrounds and life experiences, and seeking feedback from a broad set of perspectives; staff diversity data is submitted to the American Society of News Editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, clarifications and editor's notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post strives to be promptly responsive in correcting errors; use corrections, clarifications or editor’s notes to tell readers clearly and quickly what was wrong and what is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updating digital reports is normal and need not always be annotated unless there is particular reason; a correction/clarification/editor’s note is necessary when correcting a significant mistake or when language was unclear; Editor’s Notes address cases that call into question the substance of an article or raise significant ethical matters and require senior editor approval. Other rules: indicate corrections found via comments in comment streams; correct erroneous alerts and social posts on those platforms; do not attribute blame to individual reporters/editors in notices (but may note production problems or bad information from trusted sources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take-down (unpublish) requests policy
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of editorial policy, The Post does not grant take-down requests except after high-level vetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject claims inaccuracy, investigate and, if necessary, publish a correction; consider updates or follow-up coverage rather than removal. Will consider take-down only in limited circumstances (e.g., person under threat of physical harm). Vet requests at highest levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on sources and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Washington Post is committed to disclosing to readers the sources of the information in its stories to the maximum possible extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is central: prefer named sources; when using unnamed sources, ensure the benefit to readers is worth the cost in credibility; editors should know identity of unnamed sources; prefer at least two independent sources for factual information based on confidential informants; a document can sometimes serve as a second source; publish single-source info only after deliberation by Executive/Managing Editors and department head; strive to explain to readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence and avoid vague attributions like 'sources' or 'informed sources'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with sources (fair treatment and practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive to treat sources fairly by putting quotations into context and summarizing arguments accurately; give subjects a reasonable opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote potentially controversial statements in complete sentences/paragraphs when possible; clarify what question was being answered when relevant; do not promise sources that we will refrain from additional reporting; avoid ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources; avoid blind quotations intended only to add color; do not use pseudonyms or mislead about identities; decisions to provide less than full names require editors' participation and explanation to readers; start interviews with presumption they are on the record; inexperienced sources should be clearly informed when they are being reported on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of material and original reporting preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Be truthful about the source of information; facts and quotations not produced by our reporting must be attributed; attribution of material from other media must be total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should be able to distinguish what the reporter saw vs what was obtained via other sources (wire services, pool reporters, e-mail, websites). The Post places premium value on original reporting and expects reporters to see as much of the story as possible; if not present at a scene, make that clear; reconstructions based on witnesses must include transparent attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules and definitions for attribution (on the record/background/deep background/off the record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish ground rules at the start: On the record = attributable by name; On background/Not for attribution = attributable to a descriptive label; Deep background = can be used but not attributed; Off the record = not for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer on-the-record interviews; be careful with background requests and seek maximum revelation; avoid deep background where possible because it prevents readers from assessing source; resist sources who refuse to reveal identity to editors; clarify terms before interviews; if a source truly means off-the-record, generally avoid using that information for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting sources and sharing information with sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Our objective is to capture words and intended meaning accurately; do not allow sources to change quotations after the fact; sharing drafts of entire stories with outside sources is against policy except in extremely rare cases with Executive/Managing Editor permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading back quotes to check accuracy is acceptable, but do not let sources alter original statements; permitting sources to add to a quotation and explaining that sequence to readers is a preferable alternative; sharing sections of stories for technical accuracy (e.g., science reporting) may be allowed, but never whole drafts without high-level permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sources: seek variety and avoid overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: We must strive always to get a rich variety of voices and avoid dependence on the same academics or public figures for reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek new specialists (women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers and those not routinely quoted) and include affected individuals (students, teachers, employees) to broaden perspectives and better reflect readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post welcomes reader contributions; nearly all articles offer comment sections and live chats, and reporters/editors are encouraged to participate as they choose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask commenters to keep tone civil and follow Discussion and Submission Guidelines; provide 24/7 moderation; indicate in comment threads when errors corrected; provide channels (Help Center, letters, op-ed form, reader representative email) for other reader contact and submissions; offer opportunity for those mentioned in reporting to have their comments highlighted.
